blocks.prompt: What a Cloud Is Really Made Of
blocks.text: A cloud looks soft, like something you could sit on. You cannot. A cloud is water. The drops are so small that it takes about a million of them to make one raindrop. When the sun warms the ground, the warm air rises. As that air goes up, it gets colder. Cold air cannot hold on to water the way warm air can. So the water turns into tiny drops, and the drops together make a cloud. Look at the puffy clouds on a sunny day. See how their bottoms are flat, and all at the same height? That flat line is where the rising air finally gets cold enough.

blocks.prompt: Why Clouds Have Flat Bottoms
blocks.text: Air is not empty. It always carries water, spread out as an invisible gas called water vapor. You cannot see it. You are breathing some right now. Warm air holds a lot of vapor. Cold air holds much less. That one rule explains almost every cloud in the sky. When the sun heats the ground, the ground heats the air above it. Warm air is light, so it rises. The higher it goes, the colder it gets. At some height, the air turns too cold to hold its vapor any longer. The vapor sticks to specks of dust and salt floating in the sky, and turns into tiny drops of liquid water. Millions of those drops together are a cloud. This is why a puffy cloud has a flat bottom. Every bit of rising air in that patch of sky turns to drops at the same height, so every cloud bottom lines up. Look up on a sunny day and you will see a whole field of clouds sitting on one invisible shelf.

blocks.prompt: The Cloud That Weighs a Million Pounds
blocks.text: Hold a cloud in your mind. It looks weightless. It is not. A single fair weather cumulus cloud, the puffy kind that drifts across a summer afternoon, holds roughly five hundred thousand kilograms of water. That is about a million pounds, or the weight of a hundred elephants, floating over your yard. So why does it not fall? It does. Every drop in that cloud is falling right now. But a cloud droplet is only about a fiftieth of a millimeter across, and something that small falls through air about as fast as a snail crawls. Meanwhile the warm air underneath is rising faster than the droplets sink. The cloud stays up the way a beach ball stays up over a fan. The droplets themselves need help to exist. Water vapor will not condense in genuinely clean air. It needs a surface: a speck of dust, a grain of sea salt, a flake of ash, a fragment of pollen. Scientists call these condensation nuclei. Every droplet in every cloud is wrapped around a tiny piece of dirt. The sky is beautiful because it is not clean. And the cloud you are looking at is not really an object. It is an event. Droplets form at its edges and evaporate away again constantly, so the cloud you see at noon shares almost no water with the cloud that was there ten minutes earlier. It keeps its shape the way a flame keeps its shape, by being remade over and over.

blocks.prompt: The Man Who Named the Clouds
blocks.text: For most of human history, clouds had no names. They were considered too changeable to classify. A thing that becomes something else while you are looking at it does not seem to hold still long enough to be given a label. In December 1802, an English pharmacist named Luke Howard stood in front of a small London science club and disagreed. Clouds do have forms, he argued. There are only a few of them, and they turn into one another in ways you can learn. He named them in Latin so that scientists in any country could use the words. Cirrus, a curl of hair, for the icy streaks scratched across the top of the sky. Cumulus, a heap, for the puffy piles of a warm afternoon. Stratus, a layer, for the flat gray sheet that seals off a dull day. Nimbus, rain, to be attached to any cloud that is emptying itself onto you. The names took hold almost immediately. Goethe, the German poet, wrote verses in Howard's honor. Painters began studying skies properly. Two centuries later, a meteorologist reading a satellite image still uses Howard's vocabulary, because he had noticed the right thing: a cloud is not a shape, it is a stage in a process, and the stages repeat. Howard's system also explains a puzzle every child asks about. Why are some clouds white and others gray? A cloud droplet scatters every color of sunlight equally, which is why cloud water looks white rather than blue or red. A thin cumulus scatters that light back at you and glows. But stack the same droplets deep enough and most of the sunlight is scattered away or absorbed before it can reach the bottom of the cloud. The underside goes gray, then charcoal. A storm cloud is not made of darker water. It is made of more water, in your way. And the rain itself is harder to arrange than it looks. Cloud droplets are so small they rarely collide, and when they do they often bounce apart. It takes roughly a million of them merging to build one ordinary raindrop. A cloud can hang over a field for an hour holding a million pounds of water and deliver not a single drop of it.

meta.templateLabel: The Cloud That Weighs a Million Pounds

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Rising air cools by expanding, not by touching anything cold
Clouds reflect sunlight, which cools the planet
Clouds also trap heat rising from the ground, which warms it
Low thick clouds cool; high thin cirrus warm
On balance, clouds cool Earth by several degrees
Cloud feedback is the largest uncertainty in climate projections

blocks.prompt: The Biggest Unknown in the Sky
blocks.text: Every cloud does two opposite things at once, and the temperature of the planet depends on which one wins. Start with what a cloud is. Air always carries water as an invisible gas. Warm air can hold a great deal of it; cold air can hold very little. When a parcel of air rises, the pressure around it drops, so the parcel expands. Expanding costs energy, and the parcel pays for it out of its own heat. This is why rising air cools without anything cooling it: it is spending itself. Keep a parcel rising and it will eventually get cold enough that it cannot hold its vapor. The vapor condenses onto floating specks of dust, salt, and ash, and a cloud appears at exactly that height. That is the whole recipe, and it is why the cumulus clouds over a field all sit on the same invisible shelf. Now the two jobs. A cloud is bright. Seen from space it is one of the whitest things on Earth, and everything it reflects is sunlight that never arrives, never warms the ground, never counts. That is a cooling effect, and it is enormous. But a cloud is also a blanket. The ground is constantly radiating heat upward as infrared light, and cloud water absorbs that heat and sends much of it back down. Anyone who has felt the difference between a clear desert night and an overcast one has measured this effect personally. That is a warming effect, and it is also enormous. Which effect wins depends, absurdly, on the cloud's height and thickness. Low, thick stratus decks are excellent mirrors and mediocre blankets, because their tops sit near the ground and stay nearly as warm as it, so they radiate away roughly as much heat as they trap. Net effect: cooling. High, thin cirrus are poor mirrors, since you can see the sun straight through them, but superb blankets, because their tops are brutally cold and leak very little energy out to space while still catching heat from below. Net effect: warming. Add every cloud on Earth together and the mirrors currently win. Taken as a whole, clouds cool this planet by several degrees. Here is the problem. Nobody knows what clouds will do next. A warmer world evaporates more water, which sounds like more clouds and more cooling, a comfortable thought. But warming also changes where clouds form, how high their tops climb, and how long the low decks over the oceans survive. If the low mirrors thin out while the high blankets thicken, the cooling shrinks and the warming feeds itself. If the reverse happens, the planet partly steadies itself. Climate scientists are candid about this. Cloud feedback is the largest single source of uncertainty in their projections, and it is a real reason the estimates arrive as ranges rather than as numbers. An individual cloud is far smaller than the grid squares a global model chops the atmosphere into, so clouds cannot be simulated directly, only approximated with rules of thumb, and different rules give different planets. It is a strange position to be in. We can predict an eclipse centuries ahead to the second. We cannot yet say with confidence what the puffy white thing over the yard will be doing in fifty years.
